name: Ivica Kostelić
milestone_by_age_26: Won his first World Cup slalom race at Aspen in November 2001 from bib 64 and clinched the 2002 slalom World Cup season title (small crystal globe).
early_history_summary: Kostelić was born in Zagreb and grew up in a family ski project led by his father Ante, who coached both Ivica and his sister Janica. He made his first FIS event start in 1994 at age 14 and his first World Cup start in 1998 at age 18. After three injury-plagued seasons, his breakthrough came in November 2001 when he won the Aspen slalom from bib 64, the first of three wins that season en route to the slalom crystal globe.
family_context_summary: Born to Ante and Marica Kostelić in Zagreb; both parents played elite-level handball. Father Ante led a family ski project, coaching both Ivica and his sister Janica, who became one of the greatest female alpine skiers in history.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Ante Kostelić was not a professional skier but took it upon himself to coach both children in skiing, creating an intensive family-based training program. Both parents had elite-level handball backgrounds, providing athletic genetics and competitive mindset.

evidence_summary: Kostelić's career was shaped by his father Ante's intensive family ski project, which coached both Ivica and his sister Janica from a young age. Both parents had elite handball backgrounds, providing athletic foundation. Ivica started FIS events at 14 and World Cup at 18, but his first three seasons were plagued by injuries. His breakthrough at age 22 came from starting bib 64 at Aspen, demonstrating deep technical skill built through years of family-directed training. The sibling dynamic with Janica, who became one of the greatest female skiers ever, provided an exceptional peer environment.

She reached the Wimbledon final in 2001 at age 19 and won her first Grand Slam at the 2003 French Open at age 21.

evidence_summary: Henin's early career was defined by her precocious tennis talent (starting at age 2, winning Junior Orange Bowl at 14, French Open junior at 15) and the sustained mentorship of coach Carlos Rodríguez from age 14 for 15 years. Her mother's death from cancer when Henin was 12 created early maturity and adversity. Despite a modest family background (father a postal worker), her technical brilliance, especially her one-handed backhand, and dedicated coaching propelled her to her first Grand Slam at 21 and world No. 1 ranking.
